metrics: efficiency: Percent Optimized (OPT@k, at least 10% faster and correct) and Speedup Rate (SP@k) [execution; 25 runs, first run excluded]; correctness: pass private tests, NC rate [execution]
benchmarks: PIE (from CodeNet): Python test 986, C++ test 994; GPT-4 run on a 10% random sample of the test set
models: CodeLlama-34b-Instruct (open, code-specialized instruct); Gemini-pro (closed); gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (closed instruct); gpt-4-1106-preview (closed instruct)
baselines: Instruction prompting, ICL (4 random shots), RAG (BM25), CoT; ablations
effect_target_headline: SP@5 on Python with GPT-4: SBLLM 209.59 vs COT 178.34; 'outperforming all baselines by 8.75% ∼ 28.06% and 1.15% ∼ 9.56%' top-5 speedup on Python and C++
effect_correctness_headline: baseline methods generate at least 27.18% incorrect code for Python. In contrast, SBLLM reduces this rate by 17.18% (ChatGPT top-1)
notes: Eligibility is borderline: this is LLM optimization of human-written slow code (PIE), which could be classed as adjacent/EC4. Here it is included because the LLM generates new code whose efficiency is measured. A Wilcoxon test against baselines is reported. The GPT-4 evaluation uses only 10% of the test set. Contamination is only argued in the threats-to-validity section. No call or token cost is reported, even though the method needs 5 samples x up to 4 iterations. Some table values (e.g., GPT-4 C++ OPT values such as 5.49, which are not multiples of 1/90) look odd and may have been garbled in extraction.

title: CortexCompile: Harnessing Cortical-Inspired Architectures for Enhanced Multi-Agent NLP Code Synthesis
technique_name: CortexCompile (cortex-inspired multi-agent code synthesis with Task Orchestration Agent)
metrics: readability-maintainability: survey score 1-5 covering readability, usability and satisfaction (human, 50 participants); correctness: % error-free execution / bug counts
benchmarks: 5 custom game development tasks (Pacman, Snake, Chess, RTS, FPS)
models: GPT-4o mini fine-tuned agents (claimed 1-9B, closed); GPT-4o (closed) as baseline
baselines: GPT-4o without fine-tuning (monolithic)
effect_target_headline: On average, CortexCompile received scores above 4.5 across all tasks, while GPT-4o's scores ranged from 3.5 to 4.2.
effect_correctness_headline: in the FPS game, CortexCompile produced code that was 92% accurate, compared to GPT-4o's 82% accuracy
notes: Readability is reported only within aggregated survey scores; per-criterion values sit in figures that are not available in the text. 'Development time' measures generation time, not the efficiency of the generated code. Implementation claims are dubious (GPT-4o Mini described as 1-9B parameters, GPT-4o as 1.8T). There is no fine-tuning data, no statistics and no artifacts. Eligibility is borderline; a reviewer should verify.

title: Measuring Code Efficiency Optimization Capabilities with ACEOB
technique_name: Fine-tuning on ACEOB efficient-inefficient pairs + NPI filter (cost-model reranking of beam/sampled candidates)
metrics: efficiency: NPI (normalized execution-time index; execution / cost-model based), IOCCB (similarity-to-reference to efficient codes); correctness: I/O pass rate (Pass@1)
benchmarks: ACEOB test set, 9,305 pairs, 289 problems (Codeforces, temporal split after May 4 2022)
models: CodeT5-small 60M open; CodeT5-base 220M open; CodeT5-large-ntp-py 770M open code; CodeGen-mono 350M open code; PolyCoder 0.4B open code; ChatGPT-3.5 closed instruct (no filter)
baselines: greedy, beam 5/10, sampling 5/10 without filter; ChatGPT
effect_target_headline: PolyCoder S10 NPI 47.84 vs S10+NPI 72.05; CodeT5-small S10 57.29 vs S10+NPI 84.74
effect_correctness_headline: CodeT5-small B10 I/O 0.46% vs B10+NPI 0.19%
notes: Efficiency metrics are custom: NPI may be based on cost-model predictions rather than measured runtime, given near-zero I/O pass rates; verify this. The text says 'PolyCoder B5+NPI ... 72.05', but the table shows 72.05 for S10+NPI. No baseline without fine-tuning is reported. Datasets are said to be released, but no URL is given. Tables are garbled.

technique_name: Prototype2Code (design linting + UI layout tree + GNN element typing + structured GPT-4 prompt for CSS)

effect_correctness_headline: SSIM 0.91 ± 0.07 vs CodeFun 0.64 ± 0.06 and Screenshot-to-code 0.58 ± 0.12
notes: LLM role limited to CSS style generation; eligibility is borderline. The readability difference is not significant; the maintainability difference is significant only vs Screenshot-to-code (p=0.02), not vs CodeFun (p=0.54). Table 3 appears garbled: the Screenshot-to-code PSNR value repeats its SSIM value (0.58 ± 0.12). Venue metadata saying 'Computability in Europe' is wrong; the paper is ASME IDETC/CIE 2024.

notes: Per-CWE tables (4, 5, 10–16) are garbled in the extraction; aggregate totals were taken from the text and from Table 6. Pass@10 for CodeGen-350M dropped slightly (9.9 base to 8.4); InCoder rose (27.7 to 29.4). Contamination was handled by filtering synthetic data with more than 75% token overlap with benchmark prompts. Artifact repository was announced as 'will be available'. A secondary result shows CodeQL report plus hint raises the GPT-4 repair rate to 83.99% on average.

technique_name: PromSec (gGAN-guided iterative prompt optimization)

Fig. 15 ablation shows CWE count 4 for PromSec vs 164/46 for ablations, but the bars are garbled. Functionality is mostly measured by a graph-similarity proxy. The pipeline also edits existing code, making it partly a repair setting, but the code is regenerated by the LLM.

notes: The security metric is a custom detector of outdated/vulnerable API usage, not a standard SAST tool. The benchmark is self-built, and each prompt was run 10 times, but no variance is reported. Table V is garbled, and one cell reports w/ 0.4861 for CodeLlama with an 85.11% reduction rate, which is inconsistent. The paper only says code will be open-sourced; no URL is given.

Each experiment was run 3 times with distinct seeds and averaged, but no variance is reported. Correctness is shown only in figures; the paper says it is mostly preserved, with slight reductions in some cases. Other headline results: 12.07% average security increase over the no-technique LM, and 7.74% on attacked models. Some table layouts in the extracted text are garbled.

title: Large Language Model Unlearning for Source Code
technique_name: PROD (Probabilistic Redistribution for Output Distribution) unlearning
metrics: security: forget quality = average of (1-BLEU vs vulnerable snippet [similarity-to-reference]) and CyberSecEval static analyzer pass rate [tool-static]; combined with utility via Pareto Dominance Ratio (PDR); human/GPT-4 pairwise perceptual win rate [human, llm-judge]
benchmarks: CyberSecEval (Purple Llama) insecure code autocomplete, 1,916 snippets, 50 CWEs; also copyrighted code (100 Stack files) and deprecated API (VersiCode-derived, 3,449 snippets); HumanEval for utility
models: CodeLlama-7B, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder-7B, open, code-specialized
baselines: Gradient Ascent, DPO, NPO, FLAT; original model
effect_target_headline: Insecurity PDR: Ours 70.4 vs NPO 24.5 (CodeLlama-7B)
notes: Security is one of three unlearning tasks. The forget metric mixes BLEU with static-analyzer pass rate, and the security results are reported mainly as PDR and plots, not as raw vulnerability rates. Only CodeLlama-7B was used for the security task; the other three models were tested on the copyright task only. Utility (HumanEval) is lower than the original model, so the correctness effect is a decline relative to no unlearning but better than the baselines. Results are averaged over 5 seeds but no variance is reported for the main results. The model was first fine-tuned on the forget data. Borderline fit to the review topic: removing memorized insecure snippets.

title: Beyond Local Code Optimization: Multi-Agent Reasoning for Software System Optimization
technique_name: Multi-agent whole-system optimization framework (component/behavior/environment summarization, analysis, optimization and performance evaluation agents)
metrics: efficiency: throughput (req/sec), average response time, P50/P90/P99 latency [execution, JMeter load test, 800,000 requests]; correctness: JUnit tests pass
benchmarks: TeaStore Java microservice application (6 services), single system
models: gpt-5.2 (closed)
baselines: Original unoptimized TeaStore
effect_target_headline: Throughput 1197.79 -> 1635.89 req/sec (+36.58%); Avg Response Time −27.81%
notes: Proof-of-concept: one system, one model, one run, no LLM baseline (comparisons with SysLLMatic, OpenCode and Codex are only planned). The LLM edits human-written code, so this is borderline with EC4/adjacent; it was included as LLM-generated performance edits. Correctness is stated as preserved via JUnit, but no numbers are given. Correctness and performance validation were run outside the automated pipeline.

title: CODMAS: A Dialectic Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Structured RTL Optimization
technique_name: CODMAS (Articulator + Hypothesis Partner dialectic agents, Domain-Specific Coding Agent with Domain Knowledge Injection, Code Evaluation Agent)
metrics: efficiency: critical path delay % improvement, power % reduction, area ratio A/A0 [tool-static synthesis, Yosys]; correctness: failure rate (syntax, functional or PPA failure) via testbench simulation [execution]
benchmarks: RTLOpt (new; 120 Verilog triples: 70 pipelining, 50 clock gating)
models: GPT-4o (closed); GPT-3.5-turbo (closed); DeepSeek-v2.5 (open); Llama-3 (open); Granite-34B-Code (open, code); CodeLlama-34B (open, code)
baselines: Zero-shot; CoDes, ReAct, Reflexion (prompting/agentic); LLM-VeriPPA; ablations w/o DA, w/o DKI, w/o CEA; shared-memory multi-agent (SMA) variant
effect_target_headline: Pipelining timing gain 25.5 (GPT-4o CODMAS) vs 15.4 LLM-VeriPPA; clock gating power 21.7 vs 9.3
effect_correctness_headline: FR 19.5 (GPT-4o pipelining CODMAS) vs 39.7 LLM-VeriPPA
notes: Hardware RTL PPA (delay, power, area) is mapped to efficiency; reviewers should check whether this fits scope. The input RTL is human-written and the LLM rewrites it, so this is optimization rather than generation from scratch. Prompts and temperature are not given. Statistical tests are claimed but the reported std values conflict (±1.2 in Table 6 vs ±0.6 in the text). No code URL is given. Table 2 is partly garbled: the human-reference row is misaligned and the ablation table columns are scrambled.

title: VeriAgent: A Tool-Integrated Multi-Agent System with Evolving Memory for PPA-Aware RTL Code Generation
technique_name: VeriAgent (Programmer/Correctness/PPA agents with evolving structured memory)
metrics: efficiency: critical path delay, area, power and Relative PPA Score = 1/(Delay×Area×Power) normalized to reference implementation [tool-static synthesis]; win rate vs. baselines
benchmarks: VerilogEval Machine/Human; RTLLM v1.1 (correctness); RTLLM v2.0 (PPA, ~44 designs)

baselines: Direct prompting; ChipSeek-R1; VeriPPA (results as reported in its paper); RTLCoder, BetterV, CodeV, OriGen, CraftRTL (correctness only); ablations

notes: The output is hardware RTL (Verilog), so PPA is treated as efficiency; this mapping is borderline, and the reviewer should check scope. No PPA number is reported for Direct prompting; the improvement is shown relative to reference designs and ChipSeek-R1. Many designs are N/A (no functionally correct, synthesizable design), so the geometric mean may be computed over different design subsets. No variance or repeated runs, no compute reporting, and no threats-to-validity section. The ablation lists 'w/o PPA Analyzer' in Table 3 but describes it as 'w/o PPA Agent' in the text.

effect_correctness_headline: RPR=0.60 vs 0.48 llm understand (GPT-5.2)
notes: The NF outcome is only an unnamed LLM-judge composite (CQ) with no validation; check whether this meets IC3. Tasks are LLM-generated from news articles and described as 'unseen'. There is no variance reporting. Datasets are only promised for release. Ablation tables are readable.

technique_name: POET (differential-testing testbench generation + power-oriented NSGA-II-style LLM evolutionary optimization)
metrics: efficiency: power (μW), area (μm²) and critical path delay (ns) from synthesis/STA [tool-static]; correctness: functional pass via simulation and equivalence checking

effect_correctness_headline: 100% functional correctness (40/40), compared to 72.5% for I/O prompting (29/40), 82.5% for CoT (33/40), and 90.0% for REvolution (36/40)
notes: Hardware RTL code. PPA is treated as efficiency. Optimizes expert-written designs, so this is borderline with the adjacent category. The paper states equal numbers of LLM calls across methods but gives no counts. Single run and single model. Table 1 is garbled in the extraction. Ablation results are reported as best-counts only. Prompts are not provided and the UCB exploration coefficient c is not given.

technique_name: EffiSkill (offline mining of Operator/Meta skills + execution-free diagnosis, skill retrieval, multi-plan composition, candidate generation)

notes: Input programs are human-written canonical solutions that the LLM optimizes; this is borderline with 'adjacent' (LLM editing of human code), but the LLM generates the evaluated code, so included. Correctness is folded into OPT@k and not reported separately. Prompts are not given in the text. Contamination is addressed only by a mining/eval overlap check. Figures 4-6 are garbled in extraction.

title: C2RustXW: Program-Structure-Aware C-to-Rust Translation via Program Analysis and LLM
technique_name: C2RustXW (structure-aware dependency-ordered translation + rule/LLM syntax repair + differential-testing semantic repair)

effect_correctness_headline: perfect SynCor across all projects and strong SemCor (78.87% on average)

Clippy warnings for C2RustXW are not always lower than the LLM baseline (PLTranslation). The abstract states 43.70% code-size reduction while the introduction states 49.60%.

Only a single model is used, which the threats section justifies by resources and contamination risk. Wilcoxon tests are reported for per-instance speedups on human-written code only. Table 3 extraction is partly garbled but the values are recoverable.

Correctness is checked only with LLM-generated tests, and the final output's correctness rate is not reported separately. Open-weight models largely failed because of tool-calling errors. Inference energy is estimated (~1.1 kWh overhead) rather than counted as calls or tokens.

No threats-to-validity section. The per-design PPA table is garbled in the extraction.

The 2026 date and the internally inconsistent software versions are suspicious and should be verified.

The 'training corpus' is claimed, yet the framework is also described as training-free. The input is compiler-generated assembly, not human-written code, which makes inclusion borderline (possible EC4/adjacent). Reviewer should check eligibility and data validity.
